extracted.intended_audience: patent counsel and applicants preparing or prosecuting patent applications in Mexico (in-house counsel and outside counsel managing global portfolios)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and enforceable requirements for drafting and prosecuting patent specifications before the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI), covering sufficiency, enablement, best method, unity, claims, abstracts, drawings, and special rules for life-sciences and computer-implemented inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content of a Mexican patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application filed with the IMPI, and any resulting patent, must contain defined content including: a numbering and detailed description of any figures in the drawings (if applicable); at least one claim; an abstract; the drawings (if applicable). For life-sciences inventions, include a copy of the deposit certificate from an IDA (Budapest Treaty) and a list of nucleotide or amino acid sequences when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Article 94, LFPPI; Article 28, RIPL). IMPI generally accepts applications that meet EPO requirements. See Life-Sciences Inventions for additional documentary requirements (deposit certificate, sequence listings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The name/title must be brief and precise and clearly indicate the nature of the invention; fantasy names, commercial indications, and distinctive signs are not acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Article 94(III), LFPPI; Article 25, RIPL). Use a concise descriptive title rather than branding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description structure and mandatory headings
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must begin with the title, specify the technical field, indicate the state of the art known to the applicant as of the filing/priority date, disclose the invention, enumerate and describe figures, indicate the best-known method, and indicate industrial application if not evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles 96 and 98, LFPPI; Article 28, RIPL. Headings should include Technical field, Background, Disclosure of invention, Deposit of biological material (if applicable). The written text may include formulas, program instructions, and tables, but drawings must be separate sheets (Article 27, RIPL).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure (sufficient description)
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must disclose the claimed invention in a sufficiently clear and complete manner to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to carry it out, including the best method known to the applicant and information supporting industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Article 94(IV), LFPPI). Sufficiency is assessed as of the effective filing date and failure can render claims invalid (Article 154(II), LFPPI). Sufficiency generally depends on the specification’s contents, not on external references; referenced but undisclosed information usually cannot satisfy sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to implement the claimed invention without undue experimentation; enablement is integrated within the sufficiency requirement in Mexico.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement focuses on whether the specification provides enough practical detail (e.g., reaction conditions, catalysts). Examiners can request clarifications or further details if feasibility is unclear; lack of enablement may lead to invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-known method (best mode) disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must indicate the best method known to the applicant for implementing the claimed invention (the best-known method), including examples and references to the drawings when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Article 94(IV), Article 28(VII), RIPL). Failure to disclose the best-known method can negatively impact sufficiency and lead to objections or invalidation. Mexican law treats this as an objective disclosure requirement rather than focusing on applicant intent; no settled case law clarifies all aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An application must relate to a single invention or a group of inventions linked by a common inventive concept (inventions sharing essential technical characteristics that contribute to the same novel solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Article 93, LFPPI). Lack of unity is addressed in examination (requirement to divide into separate applications); divisional applications may be filed while the parent is pending but cannot contain new matter or claim the same subject matter; serial divisionals are restricted; divisional patents keep original filing date and 20-year term (Articles 100–113, LFPPI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims: clarity, conciseness, and support
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be clear and concise, precisely define the subject matter for which protection is sought based on essential technical features, be supported by the description, and not exceed the description’s scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Article 94(V), LFPPI; Article 29, RIPL). Claims are interpreted as of the effective filing date using the description, drawings, sequence listings, and deposit information. Use standard technical terminology of the field to satisfy clarity (analogous to definiteness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims format and drafting preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be numbered consecutively using Arabic numerals; the first claim must be independent and refer to essential features; claims must be drafted based on the invention’s technical features; claims must not reference the description or drawings unless necessary; claims may include reference signs in parentheses for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 29, RIPL. The number of claims should correspond to the nature of the claimed invention. Chemical formulas, equations, and tables may be included when appropriate (Article 27, RIPL).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim rules and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims must reproduce and include features of the claim to which they refer and specify additional features consistent with the related claim; multiple dependent claims cannot depend on another multiple dependent claim and cannot be the basis for a claim that depends on two or more claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 97, LFPPI; Article 29, RIPL. Draft dependent claims carefully to avoid prohibited dependency structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble/characteristic-part structure (Agreement rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicable, a claim must contain a preamble indicating technical features necessary for understanding the claimed object and a characteristic part introduced by phrases like 'characterized in that' which concisely set forth the technical features to be protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Article 12 of the Agreement that Establishes the Rules for Filing Applications before IMPI. A preamble is unnecessary for self-explanatory novel products (e.g., new chemical compound). Preambles are typically helpful for mechanical inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract must be clear and concise, summarise the disclosure contained in the description, claims and the most illustrative drawing, indicate the technical field, enable understanding of the technical problem and solution and the invention’s industrial application, and preferably be between 100 and 200 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Article 99, LFPPI; Article 33, RIPL). The abstract must not state the invention’s alleged merits, value or application. It may include chemical or mathematical formulas and reference signs to drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings: when required and formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must be included when necessary to understand the invention; they must allow clear understanding of the invention’s features and parts. Photographs are allowed when drawings are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Articles 30–31, RIPL; Article 94(VII), LFPPI). If required drawings are missing, IMPI will request them with a two-month deadline or consider the application abandoned. Provisional drawings may be filed but final compliant drawings must be submitted within two months; amended drawings that introduce new matter change the filing date to the amendment date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must support claims and align with claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must provide adequate support for the claims and be drafted according to the submitted claims; claims must not exceed the description’s scope and the description should be used to interpret claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Articles 94, 96, LFPPI; Article 28, RIPL). Failure to support claims may lead to limitation or revocation of claim scope; amendments cannot introduce new subject matter not in the original filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment perspective: person of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification requirements (sufficiency, enablement, clarity) are assessed from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art (technician in the field); Mexican law does not define this person but exam practices align with international standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No statutory definition in LFPPI/RIPL; courts and practice rely on expert testimony and common general knowledge. Sufficiency and enablement are judged against what such a person could reliably and repeatedly perform without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external references and plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency generally depends on the specification’s contents, not merely on external references; referenced documents that are publicly accessible and closely related can be complementary but mere references without disclosure usually do not satisfy sufficiency. Mexican law does not require a separate plausibility test, though plausibility concerns may be addressed via enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may accept post-filing evidence in response to substantive office actions; plausibility concerns are typically managed by requiring enabling disclosure or experimental data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented and AI inventions disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented and AI inventions the description must show a clear technical solution and sufficiently disclose implementation details such as algorithms, computational processes, functional block diagrams, flowcharts, input/output specifics, and, where relevant, training datasets and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include pseudocode or detailed examples to illustrate implementation and practical applications. Examination standards are not settled and may vary by examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-sciences and biotechnology disclosure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions involving biological material that cannot be fully described in writing, the applicant must deposit the material with a recognized IDA (Budapest Treaty) before the effective filing date and include deposit details and attach the deposit certificate. Descriptions should include nucleotide/amino acid sequences and experimental data when necessary to demonstrate that the invention works as described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Article 98, LFPPI; Article 34, RIPL). Include name/address of IDA, date of deposit, deposit number, nature/characteristics of material. Experimental data are often necessary for pharmaceuticals, genetic inventions, polymorphs, and selection patents; lack of data may prompt examiner objections on sufficiency, clarity, support or inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental data and exemplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants need not provide experimental evidence for every embodiment claimed, but descriptions lacking exemplification or experimental demonstration commonly are considered unclear or insufficient; comparative examples are advisable for selection patents and where technical advantage must be shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-filing experimental evidence is commonly accepted when submitted in response to substantive objections, provided it is consistent with the original application and supports the technical effect claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding vague, subjective or comparative claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims and descriptions should avoid vague terms (e.g., 'approximately', 'around') and subjective or comparative expressions (e.g., 'greater', 'thin', 'strong') that introduce ambiguity; use specific values, ranges, and clearly defined technical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using standard terminology of the technical field increases likelihood of satisfying clarity/definiteness. Define terms in the description where ambiguity may arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of new matter and amendment limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments during prosecution cannot introduce new subject matter beyond what was disclosed in the original application; adding new matter to drawings or description may change the filing date for the amended material or be disallowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If final drawings submitted after filing introduce new matter versus provisional drawings, IMPI recognizes the date of the amended drawings as the filing date (Articles 30–31, RIPL). Divisional filings cannot add new material and cannot claim the same subject matter as original application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical prosecution and examination remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: If IMPI raises objections (clarity, enablement, support), patentees can submit additional examples, experimental data, or clarifications provided the new information is consistent with the original application; amendments may be necessary but must avoid new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare to define ambiguous terms, provide technical examples and the best-known method, and be ready to narrow claims or file divisional applications when unity objections arise. IMPI may request samples or models in unusual cases (Article 26, RIPL).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on patentability related to subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to purely abstract ideas (mathematical methods or general principles) are not allowed; the specification should demonstrate technical application and contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For computer-implemented inventions, focus on technical solution and implementation details rather than abstract functional descriptions. See Practice Note on Patent-Eligible Subject Matter (Mexico).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement preventing overbroad/genus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The description must adequately support any claimed ranges, genera or species; disclosing specific ranges or species may limit claim breadth and claims cannot generally claim a genus unless the description provides adequate support for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming broad subject matter, ensure the description contains sufficient examples, embodiments, or reasoning to support the breadth; otherwise expect examiner objections or validity challenges.
